title: YouTube Video Platform: Complete Architecture
description: Design a YouTube-scale video streaming platform with chunked upload, adaptive bitrate streaming, CDN, and recommendation engine.

data.text: Design a video streaming platform like YouTube. Users upload videos that are transcoded into multiple bitrates for adaptive streaming, browse personalized recommendations, like and comment, subscribe to channels, and watch live streams. The system must handle 500 hours of video uploaded every minute, serve 1 billion hours of video watched daily by 2 billion monthly active users, deliver <3s time-to-first-frame globally, and support adaptive quality switching based on available bandwidth.

terms.definition: HTTP Live Streaming / Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP — chop video into small segments (2-10s) fetched independently, enabling ABR.
Player dynamically selects video quality (144p to 4K) based on current download bandwidth and buffer size.
Converting uploaded raw video into multiple codecs (H.264, VP9, AV1) and resolutions for all devices and bandwidths.
Video segments cached at 200+ global PoPs; popular segments served without hitting origin storage.
Upload protocol that checkpoints progress, allowing large files to resume after network failure from the last chunk.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Upload videos (up to 256GB) via resumable chunked upload with progress tracking
Adaptive bitrate streaming via HLS/DASH manifests
Personalized home feed and recommendations using ML collaborative filtering
Like, dislike, comment (threaded), share; subscribe to channels with notifications
Live streaming with DVR (rewind up to 4 hours), live chat overlay
Chapters, subtitles/captions (auto-generated via speech recognition), timestamps
Creator analytics: views, watch time, revenue, audience demographics

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: 500 hours of video uploaded per minute (~8.3 hours/second)
1 billion hours watched daily; peak 2M concurrent streams
Time to first frame (TTFF): <3s globally; rebuffering rate <1%
Storage: 500 hrs/min × 1GB/hr × 1440 min/day ≈ 720 TB raw uploads/day; 6-10× after multi-resolution encoding ≈ 5 PB/day stored
CDN bandwidth: 1B hours × average 2Mbps bitrate = 250 PB/day served

items.question: How does adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming work?
items.answer: The player downloads a master .m3u8 manifest listing available quality levels. It monitors download speed and buffer fill rate, selecting the highest quality stream whose download speed fits within the available bandwidth. On bandwidth drop, it seamlessly switches to a lower quality segment at the next segment boundary (every 2-10 seconds).

items.question: How does YouTube's recommendation system work at a high level?
items.answer: Two-stage process: (1) Candidate generation — retrieve ~100-500 candidate videos using collaborative filtering (matrix factorisation on watch history). (2) Ranking — a deep neural network re-ranks candidates using hundreds of features: watch-time probability, click-through probability, freshness, user satisfaction signals. Final list is the home feed.

items.question: How do you handle 500 hours/minute of video upload without transcoding becoming a bottleneck?
items.answer: Transcoding is horizontally scalable — each video is an independent job. Use a distributed workflow engine (Temporal, AWS Step Functions) to orchestrate parallel encoding jobs across a fleet of GPU/CPU workers. Prioritise popular creators and apply backpressure by queuing during traffic spikes. Batch encode lower-priority resolutions asynchronously after higher resolutions are ready.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Transcoding pipeline must be async and horizontally scalable — one video produces 15+ output files
Serve via HLS/DASH with CDN — never stream from origin storage directly
ABR enables seamless quality switching as bandwidth changes, keeping rebuffering <1%
Separate upload path, transcoding cluster, and read/streaming path for independent scaling
Recommendation: two-stage (candidate generation → deep ranking) to balance speed and quality
data.takeaway: YouTube's complexity lies not in the streaming itself but in the upload → transcode → CDN distribution pipeline and the recommendation engine that determines what 2 billion users watch next.
